newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices hit 7-month lows; corn, soybeans fall.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices hit 7-month lows; corn, soybeans fall.

text.p: Oil prices fell Monday to the lowest level since last summer, led by a drop in heating oil as weather forecasts indicated the tail end of winter in the Northeast would look more like an early spring.
In other markets, corn and soybeans fell while wheat and cattle prices rose. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures ended down 1.17 points at 240.06.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for March delivery ended 2.38 cents a gallon lower at 55.47 cents a gallon, its lowest closing price since July.

"Heating oil dragged down the market since, once again, the cold weather we are going to get will only be here for two days and then it gets warm like last week," said Todd Miller, vice president and refined products trader at Morgan Stanley.
April crude oil ended 68 cents a barrel lower at $20.71, the lowest level for the closest futures contract since August.
March unleaded gasoline futures closed down 1.58 cents at 60.24 cents a gallon, its lowest price since September.

Weather Services Corp., based in Lexington, Mass., said Monday that weather would be warmer than normal this week in the Northeast, similar to last week. The region has the highest heating oil demand in the world.
Crude oil has fallen more than $2 a barrel over the last three trading sessions, with traders pointing to mild weather, weak demand for heating oil and gasoline, and adequate stocks.
"The only bull of the oil complex was gasoline. Once traders gave up on that, there was nothing left holding up the market," said Prudential Securities analyst Richard Redash.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and soybean prices fell after Agriculture Department chief economist Keith Collins told a conference in Washington that soybean acreage this year could top 65 million acres.

That figure was above an official Agriculture Department projection released earlier Monday for 64 million acres and would be the largest since 1984. The department also put season-ending stocks for soybeans next year at 230 million bushels, up 90 million bushels.
"The talk of 65 million acres in beans was higher than before and that didn't help," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "Funds didn't buy beans, and, without the big fund support, we closed lower.
March soybeans closed 7 cents a bushel lower at $7.76.
Collins also estimated 1997 corn production would total 9.63 billion bushels, compared with last year's 9.293 billion. That would make this year's crop the second biggest on record.
March corn closed 2-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.89.

Wheat bucked the lower move in other grain pits after Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told the same Washington conference that the United States was prepared to restart its Export Enhancement Programme to counter European farm subsidies.
March wheat closed 2 cents a bushel higher at $3.75.

The export programme, in which the government pays commercial exporters "bonus" payments to make U.S. prices competitive, was suspended due to soaring world grain prices for the last two years. But Glickman said his patience was running out after the European Union recently began subsidising grain exports.
"Our relationship with the European Union is particularly tenuous. We can't hold out unilaterally forever," Glickman said of the export programme.
"That's my big stick, and I'm prepared to use it if that's necessary to protect our producers from unfair competition."

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, cattle futures rose to new life-of-contract highs as traders cited expectations for further strength in cash cattle prices. April live cattle ended 0.475 cent per pound higher at 69.725 cents.

"The cattle market is advancing on the expectation that packers by midweek will be paying $1 to $2 (per hundred pounds) higher for live cash cattle," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
